Who We Are

The toolkit you wish had existed when you started.

Civic Signal is a small nonprofit with a simple premise: the knowledge it takes to organize a neighborhood should be free, practical, and written for people who are doing this work without a staff or a training budget.

Our Mission

Democracy works best when neighbors have the tools to act.

The gap between good intentions and effective organizing often comes down to information — knowing how to run a meeting that doesn't spiral, how to write a grant proposal that gets funded, how to knock on a door without feeling like a pest.

That knowledge exists. It's held by experienced organizers, community development professionals, and civic leaders — but it rarely makes it into the hands of the volunteers who are doing this work in evenings and weekends, often for the first time.

Civic Signal closes that gap. We work with experienced practitioners to turn what they know into clear, practical, shareable resources — and we publish them for free.

Free, always.

Every resource on this site is free to read, download, print, and adapt. We ask only that you credit Civic Signal when you share our materials.

Built from the field up.

We review every resource with community members doing real organizing work before we publish. Their feedback shapes the final product — not internal assumptions about what organizers need.

How We Work

Four Editorial Principles

01

Plain language, always

No jargon, no acronyms without explanation, no language that assumes the reader has a graduate degree in public administration. We write like we're explaining something to a smart friend who just moved to the neighborhood.

02

Actionable over inspirational

We are not in the business of telling you why community organizing matters. You already know. We focus on the how — step-by-step, specific, and honest about what's hard.

03

Tested in the field

Every resource gets reviewed by people who have used similar materials in real campaigns, meetings, and grant applications. We don't publish anything that hasn't survived contact with actual practice.

04

Continuously updated

Organizing environments change. Grant requirements shift. Meeting formats evolve. We revise our resources at least annually based on user feedback and changing conditions on the ground.

The People

Who Runs Civic Signal

D
Diane Okafor
Executive Director

Fifteen years running neighborhood associations in Chicago and Detroit before founding Civic Signal in 2019. Diane's frustrated by how much wheel-reinventing happens in organizing, and built this library to fix it.

T
Thomas Vásquez
Content Director

Former community development officer at the City of Portland. Tom translates the practical knowledge of experienced organizers into usable formats — checklists, guides, templates, case studies.

R
Rania El-Amin
Community Partnerships

Works with neighborhood organizations across the country to pilot and review resources before they're published. Rania's also the person who fields emails from readers — reach out through the newsletter.

J
Jerome Whitfield
Grants & Development

Jerome keeps the lights on — managing grant relationships with our funders and making sure Civic Signal stays free. He also wrote large parts of the Grant Readiness Guide, drawing on a decade of proposal work.

Support

Who funds this work

Civic Signal is funded by a combination of foundation grants and individual donors. Our current funders include the Rosewood Community Foundation, the Urban Equity Fund, and the National Neighborhood Initiative. We do not accept funding from political parties, campaigns, or corporate lobbying organizations.

Stay Connected

New resources, monthly.

We publish a new resource or case study every four to six weeks. The newsletter is the fastest way to find out — plus we share organizing tips and examples from the field that don't make it onto the website.

No spam. One email per month. Unsubscribe anytime.

Get Involved

Know something our library is missing?

The best resources come from people who've been through the work. If you've developed a tool that helped your organization — a checklist, a script, a guide, a template — and you'd like to share it with the broader community, we want to hear from you.

We review all submissions, work with contributors to adapt materials to the Civic Signal format, and publish with full attribution to the originating organization or individual.

Submit a Resource Idea

What we're looking for

Practical tools built from real organizing experience — especially in areas we don't yet cover: tenant outreach, youth engagement, multilingual materials, rural community context, and tools that center communities of color.
